title: Euenius · lines 73–76
subtitle: Euenius is furious at the trick, but he gets what he chose, and the gods give him the gift of prophecy

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: A strong phrase for outrage, which shows how bitterly Euenius feels he has been treated.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.body: His fury is set against the citizens calmly handing over what he asked for, so the reader sees the deal stand regardless.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: He learns everything at once, so the reader can imagine the shock of discovering the trick.

notes.label: Point of view
notes.body: Ὡς gives the reason as Euenius sees it, so the reader sees events through his eyes without Herodotus taking sides.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense among past tenses makes the handover brisk and final.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The sentence ends on his own choice, which reminds the reader that he got exactly what he asked for.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: Αὐτίκα echoes line 48: the gift comes as quickly as the blight did, so the reader sees the gods keep their word.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The gift is part of his very nature, which makes up for his lost eyes with a different kind of sight.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The story ends on his fame rather than his anger, so the reader is left with his reward.

notes.label: Ring structure
notes.body: His fame fulfils the gods' promise in line 57 that many would call him blessed, which rounds off the story neatly.

questions: Do you sympathise with Euenius' anger? Give reasons for and against.
Why might the gods' gift be worth more to Euenius than anything the Apollonians could give him?
What does the story of Euenius suggest about the difference between human justice and the justice of the gods?

context.body: Greek myth often pairs the loss of sight with a different kind of sight. Teiresias, the most famous seer of all, is blind: in one version Hera struck him blind and Zeus, unable to undo another god's act, gave him prophecy in return. The prophet Phineus was blinded too, and Homer's bard Demodocus in the Odyssey lost his eyes but was given the gift of song. Euenius fits this pattern: the gods cannot give back his eyes, so they give him an inner sight instead. Prophecy often ran in families in Greece, and Herodotus tells the story because Euenius' son Deiphonus was serving as a seer with the Greek fleet in 479 BC.
